questions.explanation: A queue is first in, first out: jobs join at the back and the one that waited longest is taken from the front, so the flyer prints before the banner. Taking a job before printing it would release it to a printer that never received it, and adding arrivals at the front would serve the newest job first and starve the one that waited.
questions.hint: The job that arrived first must be the first one printed.
questions.learningObjective: order the steps a first-in-first-out queue follows

options.text: Take the job that has been waiting the longest
Print that job and remove it from the waiting list
Add each arriving job to the back of the waiting list
Start once the waiting list holds at least one job

questions.explanation: Counting each colour separately gives red 3, blue 2 and green 2, which also sums to the 7 items read, and blue plus green is 2 + 2 = 4. The wrong readings treat the tally as one shared counter, as a record of only first appearances, or as the length of the whole list.
questions.hint: Build the count for one colour at a time and check that they add to 7.
questions.learningObjective: build a frequency table with a keyed count for each value

options.text: 4, since blue appears twice and green appears twice

options.misconception: a counter records only the first time a value appears
options.text: 3, since only the first entry of each colour is counted

options.misconception: one shared counter is reused for every distinct colour
options.text: 2, since the count of one colour replaces the whole tally

options.misconception: the total list length is the count for a single colour
options.text: 7, since every item in the list adds one to the tally

questions.explanation: Two lists share only their positions, so deleting a name in the first list leaves every point in the second list still there and now unlabelled. Splitting a record this way does not duplicate any data, and while one list of records keeps the pairing together, a careless edit can still break it, so parallel lists are the riskier shape by design.

questions.explanation: Adding at the end only writes past the last stored position, so existing numbers stay valid and the cost is constant. Adding at the front forces every one of the 2,000 entries to shift along by one, which is the work the wrong answers pretend does not happen. Lists are not stored back to front, and nothing re-numbers them after an append.
questions.hint: Ask which operation has to touch the entries that are already stored.
questions.learningObjective: compare the cost of appending with the cost of inserting at the front

options.text: Appending at the end, since existing positions keep their numbers

options.misconception: inserting at the front moves nothing that is already stored
options.text: Adding at the front, because nothing has to move out of the way

options.misconception: adding an item makes every stored position change its number
options.text: Appending at the end, since a list renumbers itself each time

options.misconception: lists are stored back to front, so the front slot is spare
options.text: Adding at the front, because a list stores items in reverse order
